task:
Tell me, <Ranger>, have you ever dealt with DND-players? No? Well, this technology outmoded three hundred years ago, but it is still used on some backward planets... 

The thing is that they accidentally broke the DND-player kept in the Museum of Faeyan Technology on <ToPlanet> in the <ToStar> system. And nobody on the whole planet knows how to repair it. So all the Faeyan planets are drafting rangers from the backward planets hoping to find at least one expert among them who will solve the problem. There aren't many chances though but what else can they do? All told, if you are ready to go to <ToPlanet> in <Day> days and fix the player, we'll pay you <Money> cr. Is it a deal?
success:
Good job, <Ranger>! We were informed that the DND-player chews no more than 10% of all the disks. Oh, no, don't worry, this is not a problem, the percentage is quite normal due to the player's configuration peculiarities. Nothing can be done about it, it's antique, you know... 

In short, here is your <Money> cr, and thank you again!
loc.1.0:
A decently dressed Faeyan met you near the spaceport. He introduced himself as the director of the Museum of Faeyan Technology (as usual, you let his name go by). He was as kind as to offer you a drive to the museum in his personal aerocar and explained the problem to you en route. 

- The DND-player from the Museum of Faeyan Technology is famous for being the first player invented by the Faeyans. And it works very well despite its old age! Unfortunately, some strange <clr> failure <clrEnd> happened to it not long ago (I suspect that one of those disgusting tourists tried to play a pirate disk on our DND-player, which caused all the trouble!), and now it chews <clr>95%<clrEnd> of all the played disks. It has already chewed {[5..20]} disks!!! As long as DND-disks are expensive rarities themselves these days, we ought to take measures and have the player fixed. We even have a special device for this - <clr>tuner<clrEnd> and the manual, but no expert to do it.
loc.2.0: - The device has <clr>a square indicator 3*3 boxes in size<clrEnd>. After we hook the tuner up to the player and push the button, we set <clr>the overtone<clrEnd>. That is all the boxes are sort of <clr>painted in two colours - black and white <clrEnd>. There are two types of overtones. In the first of them <clr>the black boxes are organised in a square 2*2 boxes in size<clrEnd>, and in the second one <clr>they form a vertical line of three boxes <clrEnd>. The problem is in defining the overtone type.(that is, find out if it's a square or a line because their exact order is not important at all). The tuner lets one find out the colour of any <clr>two<clrEnd> boxes. The manual says that it's quite enough for the experts to define the overtone type, but it doesn't give even a hint to how one can do it. If you know the overtone type, all you need to do is just to push the other button, and the further tuning will be done automatically. Unfortunately, if one chooses the wrong overtone type, the further tuning can destroy the player completely. Taking into consideration the unicity of this particular DND-player, <clr>we don't let anybody do the further tuning if there is just a small possibility of damaging it<clrEnd>.
loc.3.0:
Awkward silence settled in the car for some time.

- Also I must warn you, that the tuner is rather old itself, and its <clr> checking function for box №9 doesn't work <clrEnd>. I hope it won't cause you any problems in defining the overtone type, - he added with complete equanimity. Both of you kept silent for the rest of the drive.

Soon you arrived to the museum. You were accompanied to the room with the DND-player. The tuner was already hooked up to it. The director of the museum ceremonially pushed the button setting the overtone.

loc.11.0: - I was reluctant to tell you about it but as long as you asked... See, we didn't have any tuners for DND-players by that time already so we had to buy one from the Pelengs. Now we suspect that its overtone primary setting system failed. It means that <clr>the overtone is set not after you push the button but only after the tuning expert picks up the first box for testing <clrEnd>. We also suspect that those nasty Pelengs re-adjusted the setting so that <clr>the overtone was set in the most inconvenient manner <clrEnd>. What else will explain bad luck of your {[2..9]}{[2..4]} predecessors? One way or another, the manual says that a true expert should be able to tune even the player with the failed overtone primary setting system.
